parts.problemMd:
When solid sodium chloride is mixed with water, sodium chloride solution forms.

What name is given to the process of mixing a solid with water to form a solution?

| **A** | Crystallising |
|---|---|
| **B** | Diluting |
| **C** | Dissolving |
| **D** | Melting |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C ****because:**

- When a solute mixes with water, it will dissolve forming a solution
- Solid sodium chloride is the solute

**A** is incorrect as crystallising is the formation of a solid (crystal) from a solution by evaporation

**B** is incorrect as diluting involves the addition of water to a solution

**D** is incorrect as melting is the process of turning a solid into a liquid

parts.problemMd:
Different salts can be prepared by titrating an alkali with an aqueous acid.

Three pieces of apparatus, **P**, **Q** and **R**, used to measure volumes of liquid are shown below.

![fig-1-q1b-1cho-1f-paper-1-nov-2021](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-science-co-ordinated-sciences-double-award-23-chemistry/acids-bases-and-salts/preparation-of-salts/assets/002-fig-1-q1b-1cho-1f-paper-1-nov-2021.png)

What are the names of the three pieces of apparatus, **P**, **Q** and **R**?

| ** ** | **P** | **Q** | **R** |
|---|---|---|---|
| ** A** | pipette | burette | measuring cylinder |
| ** B** | burette | pipette | conical flask |
| ** C** | pipette | volumetric flask | burette |
| ** D** | burette | pipette | measuring cylinder |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D ****because:**

- **P** is a burette, it is used to add varying volumes which can be measured to a high degree of accuracy
- **Q** is a pipette, it is used to measure a specific quantity of liquid to a high degree of accuracy
- **R** is a measuring cylinder, it is used to measure volumes of liquids but the degree of accuracy is not as high as using a pipette or burette

**A** is incorrect as the names of **P** and **Q** are the wrong way round

**B** is incorrect as **R** is not a conical flask

**C** is incorrect as all of the names are incorrect

parts.problemMd:
A student making copper sulfate crystals used the method shown.

![q6](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-science-co-ordinated-sciences-double-award-23-chemistry/acids-bases-and-salts/preparation-of-salts/assets/001-q6.png)

Unreacted copper carbonate was left over as it had been added in excess.

What is the reason for adding it in excess and what would step 3 be of this method?

| ** ** | **reason for adding in excess** | **step 3** |
|---|---|---|
| ** A** | to produce a greater amount of salt crystals | filtration |
| ** B** | to improve the colour intensity of the crystals | crystallisation |
| ** C** | to ensure all the acid reacts | filtration |
| ** D** | to increase the rate of reaction | evaporation |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- Neutralisation needs to occur and for this, the acid needs to have fully reacted with the base
- To remove the unreacted copper carbonate, the solution should be filtered as filtration separates a solid and a liquid

**A** is incorrect as the copper carbonate is in excess, it will not determine the amount of salt crystals made, this is determined by the amount of sulfuric acid used

**B** is incorrect as adding an excess will not alter the colour intensity **AND **filtration needs to occur before crystallisation

**D** is incorrect as adding copper carbonate in excess will not change the rate of reaction **AND **evaporation occurs after filtration

parts.problemMd:
When an aqueous salt is crystallised, some water can be retained within the structure of the salt.

What is the name given to the type of salt that forms?

| **A** | anhydrous salt |
|---|---|
| **B** | dehydrated salt |
| **C** | hydrated salt |
| **D** | soluble salt |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- Salts that contain water within their structure are called hydrated salts

**A** is incorrect as anhydrous salts are those that contain no water in their structure

**B** is incorrect as dehydrated means to have lost water but these salts contain water

**D** is incorrect as soluble salts are able to dissolve in water

parts.problemMd:
A student prepares pure hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid.

Which row shows the correct order of steps for this preparation?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

This option shows the steps in order for preparing **hydrated crystals of copper (II) sulphate**

1. **Add excess copper(II) oxide** to ensure all sulfuric acid reacts
2. **Filter** to remove unreacted (excess) copper(II) oxide
3. **Evaporate the filtrate** to the point of crystallisation (do not dry it because otherwise it will become anhydrous copper (II) sulphate)
4. **Cool** so hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals form

**B **& **D **are incorrect because excess copper(II) oxide (a solid) is still present in the mixture, so it needs to be removed before heating. Therefore, it must be the second step

**C **is incorrect because heating until dry removes water of crystallisation, so hydrated crystals cannot form

parts.problemMd:
A student wanted to prepare copper(II) sulfate crystals by reacting solid copper(II) oxide to a solution of hot sulfuric acid.

An extract from the method section of the experimental handout is shown below:

Add the copper(II) oxide in small amounts to the hot acid in the reaction flask and stir until it is …..**1**…... When the reaction has gone to completion the copper(II) oxide will no longer …..**2**……, …..**3**….. and …..**4**….. the solution to obtain the copper(II) sulfate crystals.

|   | **1** | **2** | **3** | **4** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | in excess | precipitate | cool | dissolve |
| **B** | in excess | dissolve | filter | cool |
| **C** | reacting | dissolve | cool | filter |
| **D** | reacting | precipitate | filter | cool |
parts.solutionMd:
**The correct answer is**** B**** because** these options are the correct steps for 1 - 4 to produce copper(II) sulfate crystals using this method.

**A**,** C** and **D** are incorrect as these options do not describe the correct method for this practical. The copper oxide must be added until it is in excess and no more dissolves before filtering the solution to remove any excess and cooling to obtain copper (II) sulfate crystals.

Which of the following methods to prepare a salt can be achieved using a burette and a pipette?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** D**** because:**

- Potassium chloride is formed by mixing potassium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid.
- Both of these reactants are **soluble** in water (forming aqueous solutions) so potassium chloride could be prepared using this method.

**A**, **B** and **C** incorrect as calcium carbonate, copper (II) oxide and zinc metal are all **insoluble** in water, so using a burette and a pipette would not be suitable to prepare salts with these reactants.

parts.problemMd:
Copper(II) sulfate can be prepared by reacting solid copper(II) carbonate with hot sulfuric acid. The alkali solid is always added in excess.

Why is the solid reactant added in excess?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** A**** because:**

- Copper(II) carbonate reacts with sulfuric acid to produce copper(II) sulfate:

  - CuCO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>→ CuSO<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O + CO<sub>2</sub>
- Copper(II) sulfate is **soluble **and is separated from the mixture by **evaporation**.
- If there is any acid remaining in the solution it would become dangerously concentrated during this phase of the preparation.
- For this reason the carbonate is added in excess to make sure that all of the acid has reacted.

**B** and **D **are incorrect as the rate of reaction and yield are not dependent on there being an excess of only one of the reactants.

**C **is incorrect as any unreacted copper(II) carbonate is removed by **filtration**.

parts.problemMd:
**Extended tier only**

What is the correct sequence of steps for the preparation of a pure sample of lead(II) iodide from solid potassium iodide and lead(II) nitrate ?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C ****because: **

- In order to make an insoluble salt such as lead(II) iodide you need to start with two solutions of salts, so the first step is dissolving
- The solutions are then mixed (suitable volumes would be measured out) and a precipitate results -  lead(II) iodide in this case
- The precipitate is removed by filtration, so the lead(II) iodide is the residue left on the filter paper
- However, it is contaminated with the other product, potassium nitrate, and any leftover reactants, so it must be rinsed with a little distilled water
- The lead(II) iodide must then be dried to remove the water

**A, B** and **D** are incorrect as these steps are in the wrong sequence

parts.problemMd:
A student is provided with solutions of dilute hydrochloric acid, dilute sulfuric acid, solid magnesium oxide, zinc carbonate and copper.

How many different salts could the student make?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** C**** because:**

- Copper salts cannot be made as copper is unreactive and will not react with dilute acids.
- Magnesium oxide will react with both acids producing **magnesium sulfate **and **magnesium** **chloride**:

  - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + MgO → MgSO<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O
  - 2HCl + MgO → MgCl<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O
- Zinc carbonate will also react with both acids producing **zinc** **sulfate** and **zinc** **chloride**:

  - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + ZnCO<sub>3</sub> → ZnSO<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O + CO<sub>2</sub>
  - 2HCl + ZnCO<sub>3</sub> → ZnCl<sub>2</sub> + CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O

**A**,** B** and **D** are incorrect as there are** four** salts which can be produced from the chemicals available.

parts.problemMd:
A substance reacts with dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> to form a salt which is separated by filtration.

What is the substance?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** B**** **

- Aqueous barium chloride reacts with sulfuric acid to form a white precipitate of barium sulfate:

BaCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → BaSO<sub>4</sub> (s) + 2HCl (aq)

- Barium sulfate is **insoluble** and hence can be removed by filtration.

**A **is incorrect as sodium hydroxide reacts to form sodium sulfate and all sodium salts are **soluble**

**C** is incorrect as copper metal is unreactive and does not react with dilute sulfuric acid

**D **are incorrect as copper(II) carbonate reacts to form copper(II) sulfate, which is a soluble salt

Which statement about the preparation is correct?

name: The Characteristic Properties of Acids & Bases

parts.problemMd:
Most insect bites cause a stinging sensation because of the injection of a weak acid into the surface of the skin. Which substance could be used to neutralise the acid from an insect bite?

|   | **substance** | **pH** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | battery acid | 1 |
| **B** | toothpaste | 8 |
| **C** | grill cleaner | 13 |
| **D** | lime juice | 3 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** B**** because:**

- Weak acids are neutralised by **weak** **bases**.
- Toothpaste has a pH of 8 and is the safest option as it won't harm skin which is **pH neutral**.

**A** and **D **are incorrect as these are **acidic substances** and will only further aggravate the problem.

**C **is incorrect as grill cleaner is **too abrasive** due to its high pH.

parts.problemMd:
Hydrochloric acid is often used to clean metals by reacting with the surface coating which develops on some metals when exposed to the atmosphere.

Which row correctly describes the surface coating on these metals?

|   | **name** | **acidic or basic** | **reacts with** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | oxide | basic | acid |
| **B** | oxide | acidic | basic |
| **C** | alloy | acidic | basic |
| **D** | alloy | basic | acid |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** A**** because:**

- Some metals react with oxygen in the air forming a **metal oxide** on their surface.
- Metal oxides are **basic** substances and react with **acids** to form salt and water.

**B **is incorrect as metal oxides are **basic** and react with acids.

**C **and **D **are incorrect as alloys are **mixtures** of metals with other metals or with other nonmetals such as carbon.

parts.problemMd:
Calcium reacts with sulfuric acid to form the salt, calcium sulfate, and another product.

What is the other product?

| **A** | Oxygen |
|---|---|
| **B** | Hydrogen |
| **C** | Water |
| **D** | Carbon dioxide |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- When a metal reacts with an acid, a salt and hydrogen are produced
- In this reaction:

  - calcium + sulfuric acid → calcium sulfate + hydrogen

**A** is incorrect as oxygen is not a product formed when a salt is formed

**C** is incorrect as water is formed when a metal oxide or hydroxide reacts with an acid

**D** is incorrect as carbon dioxide is formed when a metal carbonate reacts with an acid

parts.problemMd:
Which words complete the gaps 1 & 2 in these sentences?

Aqueous solutions of acids contain <u>         1         </u> ions and aqueous solutions of alkalis contain <u>         2         </u> ions.

| ** ** | 1 | 2 |
|---|---|---|
| ** A** | Na<sup>+</sup> | OH<sup>–</sup> |
| ** B** | OH<sup>–</sup> | H<sup>+</sup> |
| ** C** | H<sup>+</sup> | Cl<sup>–</sup> |
| ** D** | H<sup>+</sup> | OH<sup>–</sup> |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D ****because:**

- H<sup>+</sup> ions are released when an acid is added to water

  - e.g. HCl → H<sup>+</sup> + Cl<sup>–</sup>
- OH<sup>–</sup> ions are released when alkalis, such as NaOH, are added to water

  - e.g. NaOH → Na + OH<sup>–</sup>

**A** is incorrect as acids do not contain Na<sup>+</sup>

**B** is incorrect as the ions are correct but in the wrong order

**C** is incorrect as Cl<sup>–</sup> are only released when hydrochloric acid is added to water

Indicators are substances that change colour when they are added to acidic or alkaline solutions.

| **methyl orange** | red | orange |

Which indicator displays the correct colour in each solution?

- Litmus is red in acids and blue in alkalis

**A** is incorrect as methyl orange is red in acids and yellow in alkalis

**C** is incorrect as thymolphthalein is colourless in acids and blue in alkalis

**D** is incorrect as universal indicator is green in neutral substances

parts.problemMd:
A student is provided with an unmarked beaker containing a colourless solution and asked to identify it. The student decides to perform a series of reactions with the solution and record the observations.

Which of these observations is not indicative of an acid?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** C**** because:**

- Ammonium carbonate reacts with **alkalis** to produce the metal carbonate, ammonia gas and water. Ammonia gas is **colourless** and **pungent**

- An example is the reaction with sodium hydroxide:

  - (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> + 2NaOH → Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + 2NH<sub>3</sub>
- The reaction is** not characteristic **of an acid as an acid-base neutralisation reaction produces a salt and water only.

**A** is incorrect as acids have pH values of **below 7** and will turn blue litmus paper **red**.

**B **is incorrect as copper oxide is a weak base and will react with an acid forming **blue** hydrated copper salt. For example with sulfuric acid:

CuO +H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → CuSO<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O

**D **is incorrect as magnesium reacts with acids producing the metal salt and **bubbles** of hydrogen gas. For example with hydrochloric acid:

Mg + 2HCl → MgCl<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>

- Acids have **low **pH values and bases have **high** pH values.

NH<sub>4</sub>Cl + NaOH → **NH**<sub>**3**</sub> + NaCl + H<sub>2</sub>O

**B** is incorrect as acid-base reactions are **neutralisation **reactions.

CaCO<sub>3</sub> + 2HCl → CaCl<sub>2</sub> + **CO**<sub>**2**</sub><sub> </sub>+ H<sub>2</sub>O

parts.problemMd:
A student was given an unknown substance and asked to analyse it. The student decided to perform three tests and recorded the results as shown below.

| **1** | On heating with ammonium chloride a gas is released. |
|---|---|
| **2** | The substance turns methyl orange yellow. |
| **3** | The substance does not react with potassium carbonate. |

What kind of substance was the student given?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** C**** because:**

- Ammonium chloride, NH<sub>4</sub>Cl, when reacted with a base will produce **ammonia gas**, salt and water:

- NH<sub>4</sub>Cl(aq) + X-OH(aq) → NH<sub>3</sub>(g) + H<sub>2</sub>O(l) + XCl(aq)

- Methyl orange indicator turned yellow which means the substance is a base.

**A** and **B** are incorrect as salts and metals are **neutral compounds** and do not cause a colour change in methyl orange.

**D **is incorrect as potassium carbonate is a base and would react with an acid.

parts.problemMd:
A student is testing two substances, **P** and **Q**, as shown.

![q5-cie-igcse-chemistry](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-science-co-ordinated-sciences-double-award-23-chemistry/acids-bases-and-salts/the-characteristic-properties-of-acids-and-bases/assets/001-q5-cie-igcse-chemistry.png)

The results of the test are that the Universal indicator paper turns blue. What are substances **P **and **Q**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** B**** because:**

- In a reaction with an alkali and an **ammonium salt**, **ammonia** gas is produced.
- **P** and **Q** are sodium hydroxide and ammonium nitrate, which react together to produce sodium nitrate, water and **ammonia**:

  - NaOH + NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub> → NaNO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O + **NH**<sub>**3**</sub>
- Ammonia gas is **alkaline** and turns damp Universal Indicator paper **blue**.

**A** is incorrect as ammonium nitrate is a slightly acidic salt hence it will not react with another acid.

**C** is incorrect as sodium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid to produce sodium chloride, water and carbon dioxide gas:

Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H<sub>2</sub>O + CO<sub>2</sub>

CO<sub>2</sub> gas is very slightly acidic and hence will not turn the indicator paper blue.

**D** is incorrect as both substances are alkaline and so do not react together.

parts.problemMd:
A student gradually added excess potassium hydroxide from a burette to a conical flask containing sulfuric acid as part of a rate of reaction investigation.

Which statement describes the change in pH of the sulfuric acid as the aqueous potassium hydroxide was added?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** D**** because:**

- Potassium hydroxide is a **strong base** and reacts with sulfuric acid to produce salt and water:

  - 2 KOH + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2 H<sub>2</sub>O
- At the beginning of the reaction and before any alkali has been added the pH of the sulfuric acid is 1.
- As the alkali is added and neutralisation begins, more and more of the acid is neutralised as the alkali is added and the pH rises.
- As the alkali is added in **excess**, the pH continues to rise until it reaches pH 14 which indicates a **strong alkaline** solution.

**A** and **B **are** **incorrect as the pH of the acid increases from 1 to 14 as more alkali is added

**C **is incorrect as if the alkali is added in excess then the pH increases beyond neutrality

parts.problemMd: Which of the following elements forms an oxide that can be used to neutralise an alkaline solution?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** A**** because:**

- Nitrogen is a non metal element and hence forms an **acidic oxide.**
- The acidic oxide is water soluble and can be used to produce an acidic solution that can neutralise an alkaline solution.

**B** and **C** are incorrect as magnesium and iron are both metals and form **basic** oxides.

**D **is incorrect as helium is a noble gas and does not form oxides.

parts.problemMd: Which equation does **not** show the correct reaction of an acid?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- When a metal carbonate and acid react, a salt, carbon dioxide and water are formed
- In option B, the formula for calcium nitrate is wrong and the equation is not balanced
- The correct equation is:

CaCO<sub>3</sub> + 2HNO<sub>3</sub> → Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + CO<sub>2 </sub>+ H<sub>2</sub>O

- The correct formula for calcium nitrate is Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>

parts.problemMd:

- Element Q has an atomic number of 9, so its electronic configuration is 2,7.

parts.solutionMd:

  - 12 electrons mean an electronic configuration of 2,8,2
  
    - This means that the element is in Period 3

parts.problemMd: Element X contains 4 electrons in its outer shell and 125 neutrons in its nucleus. What is element X?

- X is in Group **IV **so has four electrons in its outer shell.
- X also has **125 neutrons**, which corresponds to lead (Pb) only (as lead has a mass number of 207 and an atomic number of 82, so  207- 82 = 125 neutrons).

**A** is incorrect as beryllium has 2 electrons in its outer shell and carbon has 4 in its outer shell.

parts.problemMd:

| **D** | 1 - | 2, 8, 8, 2 | 1 + | 2, 6 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** B**** because:**

- K donates its single outer shell electron, which means

  - It becomes a **positive** ion with a 1+ charge
  - The electronic configuration of the ion is **2, 8, 8.**
- The atomic number of F is 9 and its electronic configuration is 2, 7.
- F accepts the electron from potassium and achieves a full outer shell, which means

  - It becomes a **negative ion** with a 1- charge
  - The electronic configuration of the ion is **2, 8.**

**A** and **D **are incorrect as the charges on each ion are incorrect.

**C **is incorrect as the electronic configurations shown for each ion are incorrect.

parts.problemMd:

parts.problemMd: What change occurs to an atom when it forms a negative ion?

The table shows the change in temperature of four different reactions W, X, Y and Z.

|   | initial  temperature / ** **°C | final  temperature / ** **°C |
|---|---|---|
| **W** | 10 | 20 |
| **X** | 23 | 25 |
| **Y** | 15 | 13 |
| **Z** | 22 | 12 |

Which row  is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

There is an **increase in temperature **in **exothermic **reactions, while there is a **decrease in temperature **in **endothermic **reactions

- Work out the change in temperature for each reaction $c h a n g e i n t e m p e r a t u r e ( \Delta T ) = f i n a l t e m p e r a t u r e - i n i t i a l t e m p e r a t u r e$
- Temperature change for W $c h a n g e i n t e m p e r a t u r e ( \Delta T ) = 20 - 10 = 10 ^{\circ} C$
- Temperature change for X $c h a n g e i n t e m p e r a t u r e ( \Delta T ) = 25 - 23 = 2 ^{\circ} C$
- Temperature change for Y $c h a n g e i n t e m p e r a t u r e ( \Delta T ) = 13 - 15 = - 2 ^{\circ} C$
- Temperature change for Z $c h a n g e i n t e m p e r a t u r e ( \Delta T ) = 12 - 22 = - 10 ^{\circ} C$
- W has the **largest positive temperature increase** (**+10 °C**), so it releases the most amount of energy to the surroundings
- Therefore, **W is the most exothermic reaction**

**B** is incorrect because both W and X increase in temperature, so they are exothermic, not endothermic

**C **is incorrect because Z has a temperature decrease (−10°C), so it is endothermic

**D **is incorrect because both Y and Z decrease in temperature, so they are endothermic, not exothermic

Graph C: Two curves start at the origin but level off at different final volumes. Experiment 1 levels off at a higher volume than Experiment 2, and has a steeper initial slope.

Graph D: Two curves start at the origin and level off at different final volumes. Experiment 2 levels off at a higher volume than Experiment 1 and has the steeper initial slope.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-science-co-ordinated-sciences-double-award-23-chemistry/chemical-reactions/chemical-change-and-rate-of-reaction/assets/002-four-graphs-labelled-a-b-c-and-d-each-graph-has-.png)

**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- **Oxidation is the gain of oxygen**
- **Carbon monoxide, CO, gains oxygen from iron(III) oxide, Fe**<sub>**2**</sub>**O**<sub>**3**</sub>**, to form carbon dioxide, CO**<sub>**2**</sub>

> *A**, **B **and** D **are incorrect as the substances underlined are all losing oxygen, therefore they are reduced*

parts.problemMd:
Three reactions are shown below.

NO + O<sub>3</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub>

2C + O<sub>2</sub> → 2CO

2MgO + O<sub>2</sub> → 2MgO<sub>2</sub>

Which row correctly describes the process each reactant molecule undergoes?

|   | **NO** | **O**<sub>**3**</sub> | **MgO** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | oxidised | reduced | oxidised |
| **B** | oxidised | oxidised | reduced |
| **C** | reduced | oxidised | oxidised |
| **D** | reduced | reduced | oxidised |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** A**** because:**

- For NO and MgO, oxygen has been added so they are **oxidised**:

NO → NO<sub>2</sub>            MgO → MgO<sub>2</sub>

- For O<sub>3</sub>, oxygen has been removed so it has been **reduced**:

O<sub>3</sub> → O<sub>2</sub>

**B**,** C** and **D** are incorrect as these options do not correctly describe what happens to each reactant molecule.

parts.problemMd: What is the oxidation state of Fe in Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** D**** because:**

- Oxidation number refers to a single** atom** or **ion** which can be on their own or in a compound.
- The oxidation number of a compound is **0** and of an element is also **0**.
- The oxidation number of an ion is equal to the **charge** of that ion e.g. F<sup>ー</sup> is  -1.
- The oxidation number of **oxygen** in a compound is always **-2** (except in peroxide R-O-O-R, where it is **-1**).
- There are 3 oxygens in Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>,  so 3 x -2 = -6.
- As it is a compound, the overall charge must be 0, hence each Fe atom must be +3 since 2 x 3 = 6  and +6 - 6 = 0.

**A**, **B** and **C** are incorrect as these options do not provide an oxidation number of 0 for the compound.

parts.problemMd:

| **B** | added | lost | increased |
| **C** | lost | added | decreased |
| **D** | added | lost | unchanged |
parts.solutionMd:
**The correct answer is**** C**** because **there are three definitions of reduction. It is a reaction in which:

- Oxygen is **removed **from an element or a compound.
- An element, ion or compound **gains** electrons.
- The oxidation state of an element or compound is **decreased**.

**A**,** B** and **D **are incorrect as these options do not correctly describe what happens during reduction.

parts.problemMd:

Which substance is reduced?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Copper(II) oxide loses oxygen to form copper metal
- Loss of oxygen is reduction, so CuO is the substance that is reduced

**B** is incorrect because hydrogen gains oxygen to form water — this is oxidation, not reduction

**C** & **D** are incorrect because Cu and H<sub>2</sub>O are products of the reaction — substances that are reduced or oxidised are always in the reactants

parts.problemMd:
Aqueous copper(II) sulfate reacts with zinc according to the equation shown.

Zn (s) + CuSO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → ZnSO<sub>4</sub> (aq) + Cu (s)

Which row correctly identifies the oxidising agent and the reducing agent in this reaction?

|   | oxidising agent | reducing agent |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | CuSO<sub>4</sub> | Zn |
| **B** | Zn | CuSO<sub>4</sub> |
| **C** | Cu | ZnSO<sub>4</sub> |
| **D** | ZnSO<sub>4</sub> | Cu |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

To identify the agents (**which are always reactants**), you must first determine what is being oxidised and what is being reduced by looking at the electron transfer or changes in oxidation number

- **Zinc (Zn) **

  - The zinc atom goes from an oxidation state of 0 in Zn (s) to +2 in  ZnSO<sub>4 </sub>(aq)
  - The oxidation number of Zn has increased, which implies that Zn has lost electrons (oxidised)
  - Since zinc is **oxidised**, the substance that is oxidised acts as the **reducing agent** because it gives electrons to the other substance forcing it to reduce
- **Copper(II) sulfate (CuSO**<sub>**4**</sub>**) **

  - The copper ion goes from an oxidation state of +2 in CuSO<sub>4 </sub>(aq) to 0 in solid Cu (s)
  - The oxidation number of Cu has decreased, which implies that Cu has gained electrons (reduced)
  - Since copper is** reduced**, the substance that is reduced acts as the **oxidising agent** because it takes electrons from the other substance forcing it to oxidise

**B** is incorrect as the agents are swapped

**C** & **D **are incorrect as oxidising and reducing agents must always be in the *reactants*

**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- Hydrogen forms positive ions and is attracted to the cathode.
- Cathodes are the negatively charged electrodes.
- In the electrolysis of concentrated HCl, hydrogen is formed at the electrode 2 as  hydrogen is the only positive ion formed and migrates towards the negatively charged cathode.
- In the electrolysis of aqueous substances, the H<sup>+</sup> and OH<sup>-</sup> ions formed from the water compete with the ions from the substance dissolved at the electrodes, where only 1 product can be formed.

parts.problemMd:
In a fuel cell ............**1**........... energy is converted to ..................**2**................ energy.

|   | **1** | **2** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | electrical | heat |
| **B** | chemical | electrical |
| **C** | potential | chemical |
| **D** | chemical | heat |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- Hydrogen and oxygen are the reactants in a fuel cell and contain energy locked up in chemical bonds so it is classed as chemical energy
- When the reaction takes place between hydrogen and oxygen that energy is released usually as heat and light
- However, in a fuel cell, the energy is converted into electrical energy and is more useful than heat and light

**A** is incorrect as electrical energy is produced not consumed in a fuel cell and heat is not produced

**C** is incorrect as potential energy is not consumed in a fuel cell and chemical energy is not produced

**D** is incorrect as heat is not produced in a fuel cell, only when hydrogen burns

- Sometimes people refer to chemical energy as a type of potential energy
- Potential energy just means stored energy and is usually a term that refers to the energy held by an object relative to others
- However, it should be clear from the context here it is the wrong conversion in option** C**

parts.problemMd:
Hydrogen-oxygen fuel cells can be used to power motor vehicles.

What is the correct balanced symbol equation for the reaction that occurs in a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- In a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell, hydrogen and oxygen react together to form water
- The unbalanced equation is:

  - H<sub>2 </sub>+ O<sub>2</sub> → H<sub>2</sub>O
- Balance the oxygen atoms by putting a 2 in front of H<sub>2</sub>O:

  - H<sub>2 </sub>+ O<sub>2</sub> → **2**H<sub>2</sub>O
- Now balance the hydrogen atoms:

  - **2**H<sub>2 </sub>+ O<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O

**A** is incorrect as water is not a reactant and hydrogen and oxygen are not products. The equation is also unbalanced

**B** is incorrect as the equation is unbalanced as there are not enough H atoms on the left-hand side

**D** is incorrect as the equation is the original unbalanced equation for the reaction

parts.problemMd:
Three statements comparing gasoline (petrol) combustion engines with hydrogen-oxygen fuel cells are shown

1. The combustion of gasoline and the formation of water are both exothermic processes with a positive enthalpy change, Δ*H.*
2. Combustion engines are more polluting than fuel cells because incomplete combustion produces carbon monoxide and particulates.
3. Gasoline is more difficult and expensive to store in a vehicle than hydrogen.

Which statements are correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- **Statement 1 is incorrect:**

  - While combustion and the formation of water are both  exothermic processes that releases energy, exothermic reactions always have a **negative** enthalpy change (Δ*H*)
- **Statement 2 is correct:**

  - Hydrogen-oxygen fuel cells use hydrogen and oxygen to produce electricity, with **water as the only chemical product**
  - In contrast, the incomplete combustion of carbon-containing fuels (like gasoline) releases particulates and carbon monoxide, which is a toxic gas
- **Statement 3 is incorrect:**

  - Hydrogen is a gas at room temperature and pressure
  - It requires heavy, high-pressure tanks or very low temperatures to store it as a liquid, making it significantly **more difficult and expensive to store** than liquid gasoline

parts.solutionMd:

- The ions present in the electrolysis of aqueous copper(II) sulfate are: H<sup>+</sup> and OH<sup>-</sup> (from the aqueous solution), Cu<sup>2+</sup>  and SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>
- The H<sup>+ </sup>and Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions are attracted to the cathode and the OH<sup>-</sup> and SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> ions are attracted to the anode.
- At the cathode (negative electrode) the Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions are less reactive than the hydrogen  ions and are reduced to copper metal:

  - Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2 e<sup>- </sup>→ Cu
- At the anode (positive electrode) the OH<sup>-</sup> ions are less reactive than SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> ions are oxidised to produce oxygen and water:

  - 4 OH<sup>-</sup> → O<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O + 4 e<sup>-</sup>

**C **is incorrect as the electrons do not flow in the electrolyte, it is the ions that move and carry the current.

parts.problemMd:
**Extended tier only**

Four solutions are separately electrolysed.

| **experiment** | **solution** | **electrodes** |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | dilute aqueous sodium chloride | carbon |
| **2** | aqueous copper(II) sulfate | copper |
| **3** | concentrated hydrochloric acid | carbon |
| **4** | dilute sulfuric acid | carbon |

In which two experiments is a colourless gas evolved at the anode?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- In experiment 1, oxygen gas is formed at the anode and hydrogen gas at the cathode.
- In experiment 2, copper electrodes are used rather than carbon. Copper is a metal and although unreactive it does influence the outcome at each electrode.
- The negative sulfate ions SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> from the copper sulfate and OH<sup>-</sup> ions from the water are attracted to the anode but both are too stable and so remain in solution.
- The copper anode is oxidised in preference and releases Cu<sup>2+</sup> copper ions into solution hence there is no observable product formed at the anode in experiment 2.
- The end result is a transfer of copper ions from the anode to the cathode which is why this method is used to purify copper.
- In experiment 3, chlorine gas is formed at the anode which is a yellow green colour and hydrogen gas is evolved at the cathode.
- In experiment 4 oxygen gas is formed at the anode and hydrogen gas at the cathode.

A colourless gas is formed at the anode in experiment 1 and 4 only so B is correct.

You might think that since the cathode is the negative electrode then the electrons would not move towards it as like charges repel. The cathode is the negative electrode because it is where reduction takes place (electrons are gained). When it comes to direction of electron flow in electrolysis, remember that they flow in alphabetical order: from the **A**node to the **C**athode.

parts.problemMd:
A student carries out a titration to determine the concentration of a dilute acid using a standard alkali.

Five actions in this acid-base titration are shown in the table.

| step | action |
|---|---|
| P | record the final burette reading after the end-point is reached |
| Q | transfer a measured volume of alkali into a conical flask using a volumetric pipette |
| R | add a few drops of a suitable indicator to the flask |
| S | note the initial burette reading before starting the titration |
| T | carefully run the acid from the burette into the flask while swirling until a permanent colour change occurs |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

To answer this question correctly, you must apply your practical knowledge of the standard experimental sequence for an acid-base titration

- **Step 1 (Action Q):** First, a volumetric pipette is used to accurately measure a fixed volume of the standard alkali and transfer it into the conical flask
- **Step 2 (Action R):** Next, a few drops of a suitable indicator are added to the alkali in the flask so the end-point can be visualised
- **Step 3 (Action S):** Before opening the burette tap, the initial volume of the acid in the burette must be read and recorded
- **Step 4 (Action T):** The acid is carefully run from the burette into the flask while swirling, stopping exactly when the indicator permanently changes colour
- **Step 5 (Action P):** Finally, the final volume of the acid in the burette is recorded so the total titre can be calculated

The correct sequence is therefore **Q → R → S → T → P**

**B **&** C **are incorrect because the indicator was added after opening the burette tap. The indicator must be added  before opening the tap because otherwise there is no colour change, and the end point will not be seen

**D **is incorrect because it suggests adding the acid to reach the end-point before noting the initial burette reading . If the starting volume is not recorded before the acid is released, it is impossible to calculate how much acid was actually used!

He then added a small amount of aqueous ammonia to the solid-acid mixture and observed a white precipitate being formed. The precipitate dissolved in excess aqueous ammonia.

What is the identity of the white solid?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- The carbonates of zinc are insoluble in water
- All metal carbonates react with acids to produce carbon dioxide / CO<sub>2</sub> gas, salt and water
- The positive zinc ion, Zn<sup>2+</sup>, forms a white precipitate with the addition of ammonia

  - The white precipitate re-dissolves when ammonia is added in excess

**A** and **B** are incorrect as the nitrate salts are soluble

**D** is incorrect as although calcium carbonate is insoluble, it produces only a very small amount of precipitate with the addition of aqueous ammonia

choices.label: B

parts.problemMd:
Aqueous sodium hydroxide is used in chemical analysis.

Which statement about aqueous NaOH is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- Iron(II) ions react with aqueous sodium hydroxide to produce a green-coloured precipitate which is iron(II) hydroxide:

  - Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2OH<sup>–</sup> (aq) → Fe(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s)
- Iron(II) is insoluble in excess NaOH

**A** is incorrect as sodium sulfate is produced which is highly soluble, hence a precipitate is not formed

**C **is incorrect as the iron(II) hydroxide produced is insoluble in excess NaOH, hence it does not dissolve

**D** is incorrect as ammonia gas is produced which is basic, not acidic:  NH<sub>4</sub>Cl + NaOH → NaCl + NH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O

parts.problemMd: A student analysed a solution and found it to contain ions of silver and barium. What could the identity of the anion be?

- Only nitrates of both barium and silver are soluble in water

**B** and **D** are incorrect as  BaSO<sub>4</sub> is insoluble in water as are the carbonates of silver and barium

**C** is incorrect as AgCl is insoluble in water

parts.problemMd:
A student carries out an investigation on different plant extracts using paper chromatography. The experimental set-up he uses is shown below.

![q1-easy-mcq-12-2-separation-purification-cie-igcse-chemistry](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-science-co-ordinated-sciences-double-award-23-chemistry/experimental-techniques-and-chemical-analysis/separation-and-purification/assets/012-q1-easy-mcq-12-2-separation-purification-cie-igc.png)

Where should he place the samples of plant extract?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** A**** because:**

- In paper chromatography the sample spots should all go onto the **base line**.
- This is always made with a** pencil **as to use ink would contaminate the samples being analysed.

**B **is incorrect as the samples would dissolve in the solvent.

**C **and** D** are incorrect as the base line is used to measure the distances to calculate the *R*<sub>f </sub>value. If the spots are above or below this line then the calculations will be **inaccurate**.

parts.problemMd:
Paper chromatography was used to determine if a banned preservative, X, is present in four samples obtained from four different packaged foods labelled A, B, C and D.

The results of the analysis of the foodstuffs are shown in the diagram below.

Which foodstuff contains X?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** B**** because:**

- Compare the chromatogram for X by using a ruler and carefully identifying the spots which are the same distance from the baseline as X.
- Only foodstuff **B** matches so B is the one that contains X.
- **A**, **C** and** D** do not match and so do not contain the banned dye.

**A, C **and** D **are incorrect as the chromatogram from these foodstuffs do not match with that of X and so do not contain the banned preservative.

parts.problemMd:
Rocksalt is the mineral form of sodium chloride. It is known to commonly contain sodium chloride and sand along with other trace impurities.

A combination of physical changes and separation techniques can be used to produce higher purity sodium chloride and sand.

What is the correct order of physical changes and separation techniques to separate sodium chloride and sand?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- Water is added to the rocksalt to dissolve the sodium chloride
- The mixture is then filtered to remove and separate the insoluble sand
- The filtrate contains sodium chloride dissolved in water
- The sodium chloride can be separated / removed from the water by crystallisation

**A** and **B** are incorrect as melting will not separate the sodium chloride, it will produce molten sodium chloride with sand mixed in

**D** is incorrect as dissolving gets the sodium chloride into solution but it still contains sand Subsequent crystallising then undoes this physical change

parts.problemMd:
A substance was analysed and was found to have a boiling point of 450 °C.

At room temperature it is a soft grey solid.

Which temperature could be the melting point of a pure sample of the substance?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because**

- The substance is a **solid** at room temperature which is 20  °C.
- Its melting point must be above this temperature but must also be a **specific** number and **not a range** as the question states that the substance is pure.

**A** is incorrect as its melting point must be **above** room temperature so it has to be above 20 °C.

**B** and **C** are incorrect as pure substances boil at a **specific** temperature so their melting point would also be a specific temperature i.e. not a range of temperatures.

parts.problemMd:
Solid P melts at exactly 60<sup>o</sup>C and boils at exactly 310<sup>o</sup>C. Solid Q dissolves in ethanol and shows a green colour and a yellow colour when analysed using paper chromatography.

Which row is correct?

|   | **Contains only one substance** | **Contains more than one substance** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Q | P |
| **B** | Q | - |
| **C** | - | Q |
| **D** | P | Q |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** D**** because:**

- Impure substances have melting points and boiling points that fall in a **range of  temperatures** while pure substances have **exact **and** sharp** melting and boiling  points.
- Solid P has an **exact** melting point and boiling point hence it is a pure substance.
- Paper chromatography of solid Q produces two spots, indicating it must contain more than one substance.

**A **and** B **are incorrect as solid Q contains **more than one** substance.

**C **is incorrect as solid P contains only** one** substance.

parts.problemMd:
Pure H<sub>2</sub>O boils at 100 <sup>o</sup>C and freezes at 0 <sup>o</sup>C.

What is the melting point and boiling point of water after the addition of potassium chloride?

|   | Boiling point / <sup>o</sup>C | Freezing point / <sup>o</sup>C |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | 103 | -3 |
| **B** | 103 | 3 |
| **C** | 97 | -3 |
| **D** | 97 | No change |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** A**** because:**

- Potassium chloride in water is an **impurity** which affects its physical properties.
- Pure water boils at 100 ºC and freezes at 0 ºC.
- In water, potassium chloride causes the boiling point to** increase **and the freezing point to **decrease**.
- This is why salt is used to prevent icing on roads as it lowers the freezing point, making it more difficult for ice to form at temperature close to 0 ºC.

**B **and** D **are incorrect as the freezing point of water **decreases **when potassium chloride is added to it.

**C **is incorrect as the boiling point of water **increases **when potassium chloride is added to it.

- Distillation is used to **separate **two or more liquids from each other if they have **different boiling **points.
- The boiling point of ethanol is 78ºC and water is 100<sup>o</sup>C, ethanol therefore boils **before **the water does.

parts.problemMd:
The *R*<sub>f</sub> values of three different pigments are shown in the table.

| pigment | *R*<sub>f</sub> value |
|---|---|
| P | 0.43 |
| Q | 0.57 |
| R | 0.75 |

A student carries out chromatography on an unknown sample. The resulting chromatogram is shown below

![Chromatogram. Baseline at 0.0 cm. Solvent front at 7.0 cm. One sample spot at 3.0 cm above baseline. Ruler shown 0.0–7.0 cm.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-science-co-ordinated-sciences-double-award-23-chemistry/experimental-techniques-and-chemical-analysis/separation-and-purification/assets/001-chromatogram-baseline-at-0-0-cm-solvent-front-at.png)

What is the identity of the unknown pigment?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- To identify the pigment, you must calculate the *R*<sub>f</sub> value of the unknown spot using the formula:

$R_{f}=\frac{\mathrm{distance} \mathrm{travelled} \mathrm{by} \mathrm{substance}}{\mathrm{distance} \mathrm{travelled} \mathrm{by} \mathrm{solvent}}$

- Using the diagram:

![Chromatogram. Horizontal baseline at 0.0 cm. Horizontal solvent front line at 7.0 cm. One spot at 3.0 cm above baseline. Vertical arrows show 3.0 cm (spot) and 7.0 cm (solvent front).](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-science-co-ordinated-sciences-double-award-23-chemistry/experimental-techniques-and-chemical-analysis/separation-and-purification/assets/002-chromatogram-horizontal-baseline-at-0-0-cm-horiz.png)

- Distance travelled by substance = 3.0 cm
- Distance travelled by solvent (solvent front) = 7.0 cm

$R_{f}=\frac{3.0}{7.0}=0.428..=0.43$

- Comparing this to the table, the unknown sample matches **pigment P **

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always measure the distance from the **baseline to the centre of the spot**, not the top or bottom. Using the centre of the spot ensures accurate **Rf values** and avoids losing marks for measurement errors.

parts.problemMd: A yellow solid, W is soluble in water. Which method of separation can be used to obtain the solid W from an aqueous solution?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** D**** because:**

- Crystallisation is a separation technique used to separate a **soluble solid** from a  solution.
- It involves evaporating the solution to a much smaller volume and then leaving it to cool.
- As the solution cools, crystals of the solid form.

**A **is incorrect as neutralisation is the reaction between an **acid **and a **base** and is not a separation technique.

**B **is incorrect as chromatography is useful for separating a mixture of **dissolved** substances.

**C** is incorrect as distillation is used to separate a **pure liquid **from a **solution **or a **mixture **of liquids.

- Measure the distance from the baseline to the solvent front.
- Use the equation for the retention factor: *R*<sub>f</sub> = $\frac{distance travelled by spot}{distance travelled by solvent front}$

parts.problemMd:
Many metals can be extracted from their ores by heating the metal oxide with carbon.

Which of these metals can’t be extracted using carbon?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because**

- Aluminium is more reactive than carbon.
- The method used to extract a metal from its ore depends on the reactivity of the metal in the **reactivity series**.
- Metals lower than **carbon **in the reactivity series can be reduced by heating with carbon.
- Metals above carbon in the reactivity series will either need to be reduced by another more reactive element or extracted via electrolysis.
- Extraction by electrolysis is used to extract aluminium.

**A,** **B** and **D **are incorrect as zinc, copper and iron are all below carbon in the reactivity series and can be extracted by reduction with carbon.

parts.problemMd:
**Extended tier only **

The blast furnace is used to extract iron from haematite.

![q3-9-3-easy-cie-igcse-chemistry](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-science-co-ordinated-sciences-double-award-23-chemistry/metals/extraction-of-metals/assets/002-q3-9-3-easy-cie-igcse-chemistry.png)

The haematite contains silica as an impurity

What is used to react with the impurity and remove it?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- Impure iron contains impurities of carbon, phosphorus, silicon and sulfur.
- Oxygen is blown in to **oxidise** the impurities to their oxides in a basic oxygen converter.
- Calcium oxide is used to remove the silicon and phosphorus oxides to produce slag:

  - SiO<sub>2</sub> + CaO → CaSiO<sub>3</sub>
- The slag floats to the surface of the molten iron and is removed.

**A **is incorrect as carbon reacts with oxygen in a combustion reaction, heating the blast furnace forming carbon dioxide: C + O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub>

**C **is incorrect as carbon dioxide is produced in the reaction of carbon with oxygen.

**D **is incorrect as oxygen reacts with carbon in a combustion reaction, heating the blast furnace forming carbon dioxide:  C + O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub>

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: To remove impurities from the iron ore

choices.label: B

parts.problemMd:
Iron is extracted from hematite, Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, in a blast furnace. Limestone is also added to the furnace.

What is the purpose of the limestone?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** A**** because:**

- Limestone is added to remove **sand impurities** in hematite.
- It reacts with the impurities forming a **slag** which is tapped off separately from the molten iron.

**B **is incorrect as the furnace is heated by the combustion of carbon and hot air that is blasted into the furnace.

**C **is incorrect as the hematite is reduced by carbon monoxide:

Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 2CO → 2Fe + 3CO<sub>2</sub>

**D **is incorrect as the waste gases are piped to a heat exchanger to heat the incoming air.

parts.problemMd: Which of the following metals can **not** be extracted from its ore by reduction?

parts.problemMd:
In a blast furnace, iron (III) oxide is converted into iron and carbon monoxide is converted into carbon dioxide, as shown in the equation:

Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>  + 3CO → 2 Fe + 3 CO<sub>2</sub>

What happens to each of these reactants?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A**** because**

- The carbon monoxide is **oxidised** as it gains oxygen:

  - 3CO → 3CO<sub>2</sub>
- Iron (III) oxide is **reduced **as it loses oxygen:

  - Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> → 2Fe

**B **is incorrect as carbon monoxide is oxidised, oxygen is added to make it carbon dioxide and iron (III) oxide is reduced as oxygen is removed.

**C **is incorrect as iron (III) oxide is reduced as oxygen is removed

**D **is incorrect as carbon monoxide is oxidised; oxygen is added to make it carbon dioxide.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows how aluminium is manufactured by electrolysis.

![q2-9-3-medium-cie-igcse-chemistry](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-science-co-ordinated-sciences-double-award-23-chemistry/metals/extraction-of-metals/assets/001-q2-9-3-medium-cie-igcse-chemistry.png)

What are the anode and cathode made of?

|   | **anode** | **cathode** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | aluminium | aluminium |
| **B** | aluminium | graphite |
| **C** | graphite | aluminium |
| **D** | graphite | graphite |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- In the electrolysis of aluminium, both electrodes are made from graphite.
- Graphite is an allotrope of carbon which is chemically inert and resistant to corrosion but does conduct heat and electricity, so the flow of electricity and heat is maintained while the electrodes do not interfere with the chemistry of the process.

**A, B** and **C** are incorrect as aluminium is a metal which has different properties than graphite and would participate in the chemistry of the process and hence interrupt the extraction.

parts.problemMd:
Aluminium is extracted from its oxide by electrolysis.

The oxide is dissolved in ……**1**…… cryolite and aluminium is deposited at the ……**2**……

Which words correctly complete gaps 1 and 2?

|   | **1** | **2** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | aqueous | cathode |
| **B** | aqueous | anode |
| **C** | molten | cathode |
| **D** | molten | anode |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- The melting point of aluminium oxide is 2030ºC.
- By dissolving it in molten cryolite, the melting point is reduced to 900 - 1000ºC.

parts.problemMd: Which word equation represents the rusting of iron?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Rusting is an oxidation reaction

  - Iron reacts with oxygen in the presence of** water **and** air**
  
    - Both of them are necessary, otherwise, the rusting process will not occur

    - loses electrons to oxygen forming iron(III) ions

parts.problemMd:
Four metals, **P**, **Q**, **R**, and **S**, are each placed in separate test tubes containing dilute hydrochloric acid. The observations are recorded in the table below.

| **metal** | **observation with dilute hydrochloric acid** |
|---|---|
| **P** | no reaction |
| **Q** | slow bubbles of gas produced |
| **R** | rapid bubbling, test tube becomes warm |
| **S** | moderate bubbles of gas produced |

Which row shows the correct order of reactivity **and** correctly identifies the metal that is copper?

|   | **order of reactivity (most  to least)** | **copper** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | R, S, Q, P | P |
| **B** | R, S, Q, P | Q |
| **C** | P, Q, S, R | P |
| **D** | R, Q, S, P | P |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

The more vigorous the reaction (faster bubbling and heat produced), the more reactive the metal:

- **R** is the most reactive because it shows rapid bubbling and the reaction is exothermic (test tube becomes warm)
- **S** is next with moderate bubbling
- **Q** is less reactive with slow bubbling
- **P** is the least reactive as there is no reaction

This gives the order: R (most) → S → Q → P (least)

In the reactivity series, metals below hydrogen do not react with dilute acids to produce hydrogen gas. Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series. Since metal P showed no reaction, P is copper.

**B** is incorrect as although the reactivity order is correct, Q reacts slowly with the acid, so it cannot be copper

**C** is incorrect as the reactivity order is reversed; the metal with no reaction (P) is placed as most reactive

**D** is incorrect as the reactivity order places Q above S, but S produces moderate bubbles while Q produces only slow bubbles

> **[exam-tip]**
> Metals below hydrogen in the reactivity series do not react with dilute acids. Copper, silver and gold are all below hydrogen.
> 
> The vigour of the reaction (rate of bubbling, temperature rise) indicates relative reactivity.

- Carbon dioxide is formed with a plentiful supply of oxygen, during complete combustion
- Carbon monoxide is formed with a limited supply of oxygen
- Carbon is formed with a **very** limited supply of oxygen

  - Exam questions will sometimes indicate if the product of incomplete combustion is carbon monoxide or carbon

**A **is incorrect as this is the balanced symbol equation for the **complete** **combustion** of methane

**C **is incorrect as hydrogen is not a product of the combustion of alkanes

**D **is incorrect as this is not a balanced equation and has hydrogen gas as a product.

| **B** | thermal decomposition | paraffin |

parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- The industrial process is **fractional** **distillation**.
- Fractional distillation separates the hydrocarbons in crude oil based on the **boiling points**. The boiling points are different due to the molecular mass.

**A **is incorrect as the substance is not petrol, petrol is not used in aircraft as a fuel.

**B **and** D  **are incorrect as the industrial process is not thermal decomposition. Fractional distillation does not break the molecules but separates the mixture based on boiling point.

parts.problemMd:
Petroleum is separated into fractions by fractional distillation.

Which statement about the properties of the fractions is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Crude oil (petroleum) is a mixture of hydrocarbons with different chain lengths
- In **fractional distillation**, crude oil is heated so that most of it vaporises
- The vapours enter a **fractionating column**, which is **hot at the bottom and cooler at the top**

  - Hydrocarbons with **high boiling points** (long-chain molecules) **condense low down** in the column
  - Hydrocarbons with **low boiling points** (short-chain molecules) **rise higher** before condensing
- As chain length increases, hydrocarbons have **stronger intermolecular forces**

  - Stronger intermolecular forces mean **higher boiling points**, **higher viscosity**, and **lower volatility**
  - This explains why fractions with longer carbon chains are more viscous liquids
- Therefore, the viscosity of the fractions increases as chain length increases, so C is correct

**A **is incorrect because fractions with more carbon atoms have higher boiling points, not lower. This is because larger molecules have strong intermolecular forces of attraction

**B **is incorrect because fractions with small molecules have low boiling points and rise to the top of the fractionating column

**D **is incorrect because refinery gases contain short-chain hydrocarbons, which are more volatile than long-chain hydrocarbons

A student carried out a cracking reaction on hydrocarbon,** P**, and obtained two products; **Q** and **R**.

![q2-11-2-medium-cie-igcse-chemistry](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-science-co-ordinated-sciences-double-award-23-chemistry/organic-chemistry/organic-families/assets/006-q2-11-2-medium-cie-igcse-chemistry.png)

The student then made the following notes:

| **1** | **Q** is unsaturated. |
|---|---|
| **2** | **R** will decolourise bromine water. |
| **3** | A molecule of** P** has 7 carbon atoms. |

Which of the statements are correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- **R** will decolourise bromine water.
- Compound **R** is an **alkene** with a **carbon carbon double bond**.
- This will react with the **bromine water** in a **halogenation** reaction.
- **P** has** 7** carbon atoms:

  - The process of **cracking** involves breaking large **hydrocarbon ** molecules into smaller molecules.
  - The total number of carbon atoms in the two smaller molecules is **7**. Carbon atoms are not lost in the reaction.

**A, B** and **D **are incorrect as Q is not unsaturated, this has no **carbon carbon double bonds**. Q will be an alkane, butane.

parts.problemMd:
Which of the following properties of different compounds in petroleum enable it to be separated into fractions?

| ** ** | **1** | Chain length |
|---|---|---|
| ** ** | **2** | Chemical reactivity |
| ** ** | **3** | Solubility in water |
| ** ** | **4** | Boiling point |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- Petroleum (crude oil) is a mixture of different hydrocarbons with different chain lengths and physical properties.
- Petroleum is separated through **fractional distillation**, which separates the molecules with similar boiling points called fractions.
- The fractions have a boiling point range; the boiling point depends on the molecular mass of the molecules.
- The **larger** the molecular **mass** the **higher** the **boiling** **point**; therefore larger molecules with high boiling points are separated at the bottom of the column.
- The shorter, lighter chains are separated at the top of the column.

**A, C** and **D ** are incorrect because chemical reactivity and solubility in water does vary with each fraction but these properties are not used to separate the mixture into fractions.

| **B** | 71 to 120 |
| **C** | 121 to 170 |
| **D** | over 171 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A**** because**

- The boiling point of the hydrocarbon depends on the **molecular** **mass**. The **larger** the molecular **mass** the **higher** the **boiling** **point**.
- Larger molecules have more **intermolecular** **forces** which hold the molecules together, so more energy is needed to overcome these forces for a state change.
- Smaller molecules have less intermolecular forces between the molecules so need less energy to overcome these forces.

**B, C** and **D ** are incorrect because they all have boiling points above A and therefore bigger molecules.

parts.problemMd:
#### Extended tier only

Which row correctly describes the mole and the value of Avogadro’s constant?

|   | **one mole of a substance is equal to** | **one mole of a substance contains** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | the substances relative atomic or molecular mass in grams | 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> atoms, molecules or formula units |
| **B** | the substances atomic number in grams | 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> atoms, molecules or formula units |
| **C** | the substances relative atomic or molecular mass in grams | 12.04 x 10<sup>23</sup> atoms, molecules or formula units |
| **D** | the substances atomic number in grams | 12.04 x 10<sup>23</sup> atoms, molecules or formula units |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A**** because:**

- One mole is the amount of a substance that contains $6.02\times10^{23}$ particles and is known as **Avogadro's constant.**
- 1 mole of oxygen, which is a diatomic molecule O<sub>2</sub>, contains $6.20\times10^{23}$ **molecules** of oxygen but $2 \times ( 6.02 \times 10^{23} )$ **atoms** of oxygen.
- One mole of any element is equal to the **relative atomic mass** of that element in **grams.** E.g. Ca has an *A*<sub>r </sub>of 40, so one mole of Ca has a mass of 40g.
- For a molecule, the relative atomic masses are **added** together. E.g. one mole of NaOH has a mass of 23 + 16 + 1 = 40g.

**B** and **D** are incorrect as the mole refers to the **mass number,** not the atomic number.

**C **is incorrect as the value of Avogadro's constant is $6.02\times10^{23}.$

parts.solutionMd:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

*n(*Mg) = $\frac{0.6}{24}$

*n(*Mg) = **0.025 moles**

- Calculate the moles of oxygen available:

1 mole of any gas occupies 24 dm<sup>3</sup>

2Mg + O<sub>2</sub> → 2MgO

**2 moles** Mg requires **1 mole **of O<sub>2</sub>

0.025 moles of Mg needs 0.0125 moles of oxygen

  - We have 0.025 moles of Mg
  - We need 0.025 moles of Mg
- Compare oxygen moles:

  - We have 0.025 moles of O<sub>2</sub>

**A**,** C **and** D **are incorrect as these options do not correctly describe the reaction.

parts.problemMd:
How many oxygen atoms are there in 10.0 g of magnesium nitrate, Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>?

(The Avogadro constant, L, is 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

**Step 1:** Calculate the relative formula mass (*M*<sub>r</sub>) of Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2 </sub>using the relative atomic masses from the Periodic Table

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 24 + (2×14) + (6×16)

*M*<sub>r</sub> =24 + 28 + 96 = 148

**Step 2:** Calculate the number of moles of Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>

$\mathrm{moles}=\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

$\mathrm{moles}=\frac{10.0g}{148g\mathrm{mol}^{-1}}$

$\mathrm{moles}=0.06757\mathrm{moles}$

**Step 3:** The fundamental unit of an ionic compound is a formula unit, therefore, the next step is calculating the number of formula units in Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>

$\mathrm{fundamental} \mathrm{units}=\mathrm{moles}\times\mathrm{Avogadro} \mathrm{constant}$

$\text{fundamental} \text{units} = 0.06757 \text{mol} \times ( 6.02 \times 10^{23} \text{mol} ^{ - } 1 )$

$\mathrm{fundamental} \mathrm{units}=4.0677\times10^{22}\mathrm{formula} \mathrm{units}$

**Step 4: **Calculate the number of oxygen atoms

According to the chemical formula**, one formula unit of Mg(NO**<sub>**3**</sub>**)**<sub>**2 **</sub>**contains 6 oxygen atoms**, therefore:

$\mathrm{number} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{oxygen} \mathrm{atoms}=\mathrm{formula} \mathrm{units}\times6$

$\mathrm{number} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{oxygen} \mathrm{atoms}=4.0677\times10^{22}\times6$

$\mathrm{number} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{oxygen} \mathrm{atoms}=2.44\times10^{23}\mathrm{oxygen} \mathrm{atoms}$

> **[exam-tip]**
> In multiple-choice calculation questions, the wrong options are often based on **common mistakes**. They usually match answers you would get if you **stop too early** or **misuse the formula**.
> 
> Always complete every step carefully and check the formula before choosing your answer!

parts.problemMd:
**X**, **Y** and **Z** are the halogens chlorine, bromine and iodine, but not necessarily in that order.

When aqueous **Y** is added to an aqueous solution containing ions of **Z**, a brown solution is formed. When aqueous **X** is added to an aqueous solution containing ions of **Z**, no reaction occurs

Which row correctly identifies halogens X, Y and Z?

|   | X | Y | Z |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | bromine | chlorine | iodine |
| **B** | iodine | chlorine | bromine |
| **C** | iodine | bromine | chlorine |
| **D** | chlorine | iodine | bromine |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Halogens are Group VII non-metals
- In terms of reactivity, a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide ion from its aqueous solution
- The reactivity decreases down the group (chlorine > bromine > iodine)
- When a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen in aqueous state, the less reactive halogen will be observed in the mixture

  - It is important to recap the  appearance of the halogens
  
    - Chlorine is a pale yellow-green gas, bromine is a red-brown liquid, and iodine is a grey-black solid (brown in solution)
- A brown solution is formed when aqueous Y is added to ions of Z

  - A brown solution in water can indicate that bromine (red-brown liquid) or iodine (typically grey solid, but brown in aqueous) was formed
  - This means that** Z is less reactive than Y**

- When aqueous X is added to Z ions, **no reaction occurs**

  - This means **X is less reactive than Z**
  - In consequence, **X is** **less reactive than Y**

- Therefore, in order of decreasing reactivity:

  - Y >  Z  >  X

- Since, reactivity decreases down the group (chlorine > bromine > iodine)

  - Y = chlorine, Z = bromine, X = iodine

parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** A**** because:**

- Elements are arranged on the Periodic table in order of **increasing atomic** **number**, where each element has one proton more than the element preceding it.
- The table is arranged in vertical columns called **Groups** numbered I - VIII and in rows called **Periods**.

**B** and **D** are incorrect as the mass number is not used to order the elements.

**C **is incorrect as the name used for columns is **Group** and for rows is **Period.**

parts.problemMd: Which property of elements increases as you move across the Periodic table?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** B**** because:**

- Elements are arranged on the Periodic table by **increasing atomic number **
- Where each element has one proton more than the element preceding it.
- Each element is neutral so as the atomic number increases by one so too does the number of **electrons**.
- Each element has one electron more than the preceding element and this electron is added to the **outer shell**.

**A** is incorrect as the number of electrons shells increases moving **down** the table but stays the same moving across.

**C **is incorrect as metallic character **decreases** as we move across the Periodic table from left to right.

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- Atoms form ions to achieve a full outer shell of electrons
- An ion with a charge of 2- has gained two electrons to do this
- Elements in Group 6 have six electrons in their outer shell so will gain two electrons to achieve 8

**A **is incorrect as Group 1 elements lose one electron to form ions with a 1+ charge

**B** is incorrect as Group 2 elements lose two electrons to form ions with a 2+ charge

- There are **patterns** in the way the elements are arranged on the Periodic table, there are also patterns and trends in the **chemical** **behaviour** of the elements.
- In this way the Periodic table can be used to predict how an unknown element will behave and was used to **identify** them.

**C **is incorrect as elements in different Groups have **different** **properties** as they have different outer shell **electron** **configurations**. Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outer shell and share similar properties.

What makes potassium more metallic than krypton?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** D**** because:**

- The change in metallic to non-metallic character as we move across the Periodic table from left to right is linked to the **electronic configuration** of the elements.
- Non-metals have **more electrons** in their outer shells than metals.
- Potassium is in **Group I **and has **1** electron in its outer shell whereas krypton is in **Group VIII** and has **8** electrons in its outer shell.

**A** and **B** are incorrect as although potassium has fewer electrons and protons than krypton, it is the **outer shell electrons** that determine its chemical properties.

parts.problemMd:

| **3** | Carbon is less metallic than beryllium. |
| **4** | Sodium is less metallic than aluminium. |
parts.solutionMd:

- Magnesium lies further to the **left** than silicon, hence it has a greater metallic character than silicon.
- Beryllium is further **left** than carbon, hence it also has greater metallic character than carbon.

**B**,** C** and **D** are incorrect as as lithium and sodium are both more metallic than boron and aluminium as they lie further on the left of the Periodic table.

- Metallic character of elements **decreases** as you move across a period and is linked to the number of outer shell electrons in each element.
- Elements on the right more **readily accept electrons** to fill their valence shells as it is easier for them to gain a small number of electrons than it is to lose a large number of them.

parts.problemMd:

Which group and period can the element be found in?

| **B** | 6 | 8 |
| **C** | 3 | 6 |
| **D** | 8 | 2 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A**** because:**

- The electronic configuration shows the arrangement of electrons in their shells
- The last notation is the number of electrons in the outer shell
- The number of electrons in the outer shell correlates to the group number

  - 2,8,**6 **shows there are six electrons in the outer shell so the element is in Group 6
- The period number refers to the number of shells an atom has
- The number of notations shows the number of shells

  - 2,8,6 has three notations so the element has three shells and is in Period 3

**B**, **C** and **D** are incorrect as the group or period number is wrong
